lessons.title: A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass and isotopes
lessons.summary: Build a working picture of the atom: elements, compounds and mixtures, how the atomic model developed, what protons, neutrons and electrons are, and how isotopes lead to relative atomic mass.
objectives: I can describe the difference between elements, compounds and mixtures and choose a suitable separation technique for a mixture.
I can balance a symbol equation and explain why no atoms are lost or made in a chemical reaction.
I can describe how the model of the atom changed from the plum pudding model to the nuclear model with neutrons.
I can work out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion from its atomic number and mass number.
I can calculate a relative atomic mass from isotope abundances and write the electronic structure of any of the first 20 elements.

activities.title: Atoms, elements, compounds and equations
activities.content:
## Atoms, elements and compounds

Everything you can touch is built from **atoms**, the smallest particles of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.

- An **element** is a substance made of only one type of atom. There are roughly 100 of them, each with a **chemical symbol**: one or two letters, the first always a capital, such as O, Na, Cl and Fe.
- A **compound** contains two or more different elements **chemically bonded** together in fixed proportions. Compounds can only be split back into elements by a chemical reaction.

A **formula** tells you exactly which atoms are present. In H₂O the small **subscript** 2 means two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom. A bracket multiplies everything inside it, so Mg(OH)₂ contains one Mg, two O and two H.

## Word and symbol equations

A chemical reaction rearranges atoms into new substances. Because **no atoms are created or destroyed**, the same number of each type of atom must appear on both sides. That is why symbol equations must be **balanced**.

- Word equation: copper + oxygen → copper oxide
- Symbol equation: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO

You balance by changing the **big numbers** in front of a formula, never the subscripts inside it. State symbols show the physical state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) dissolved in water.

activities.title: Worked example: balancing an equation
activities.content:
**Balance the equation for aluminium reacting with oxygen to form aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.**

1. Write the unbalanced equation: Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃
2. Count each element. Left: 1 Al, 2 O. Right: 2 Al, 3 O. Neither matches.
3. Fix oxygen first because it is the awkward one. The smallest number that both 2 and 3 divide into is 6, so put **3** in front of O₂ (6 O) and **2** in front of Al₂O₃ (6 O): Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃
4. Now recount aluminium. Right: 2 × 2 = 4 Al. So put **4** in front of Al on the left.
5. Final answer: **4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃**

Check: 4 Al and 6 O on each side. Balanced. Notice that the formula Al₂O₃ never changed, only the numbers in front.

question.text: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid to make magnesium chloride and hydrogen. Which equation is correctly balanced?
question.hint: Count the hydrogen and chlorine atoms on each side. MgCl₂ needs two chlorine atoms.
question.explanation: MgCl₂ contains two Cl and H₂ contains two H, so two HCl are needed on the left: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Left: 1 Mg, 2 H, 2 Cl. Right: 1 Mg, 2 Cl, 2 H.

options.feedback: There is only one Cl and one H on the left but two of each on the right.
You cannot change the formulae. Hydrogen gas is H₂ and magnesium chloride is MgCl₂.
Now there are two Mg on the left and only one on the right.

activities.title: Mixtures and how to separate them
activities.content:
## Mixtures

A **mixture** is two or more substances (elements or compounds) that are **not chemically joined**. Sea water, air and muddy water are all mixtures. Because there are no bonds between the parts, each substance keeps its own properties and the mixture can be separated by **physical processes**. No chemical reaction is needed.

## Choosing a technique

| Technique | What it separates | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Filtration** | Insoluble solid from a liquid | Liquid passes through filter paper; solid stays behind as the residue |
| **Crystallisation** | Soluble solid from its solution | Heat gently to evaporate some solvent, then leave to cool so crystals grow |
| **Simple distillation** | A solvent from a solution | Boil the liquid, then cool the vapour in a condenser so it turns back into a liquid |
| **Fractional distillation** | Liquids with different boiling points | Vapour rises up a fractionating column; the liquid with the lowest boiling point comes off first |
| **Chromatography** | Soluble substances such as dyes in ink | A solvent moves up paper carrying each substance a different distance |

The key question to ask yourself is: *is the solid soluble or insoluble, and am I trying to keep the solid or the liquid?* Keeping sand from sand and water is filtration; keeping the water from salt water is simple distillation; keeping the salt is crystallisation.

question.text: Match each mixture to the best technique for separating it.
question.hint: Ask whether the solid is soluble, and whether you want to keep the solid or the liquid.
question.explanation: Chalk is insoluble so filtration works. Pure water from salt water needs simple distillation (the water boils off and is condensed). To keep the salt you crystallise. Two miscible liquids with different boiling points need fractional distillation. Coloured dyes are separated by chromatography.

Ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) from a mixture with water
The different coloured dyes in a felt-tip pen

activities.title: How the model of the atom changed
activities.content:
## A model that kept improving

Scientists cannot see atoms directly, so they build **models** and change them when new evidence turns up.

1. **Dalton (early 1800s)**: atoms are tiny solid spheres that cannot be split.
2. **Thomson (1897)** discovered the **electron**, a particle much lighter than an atom with a negative charge. Because atoms are neutral, he pictured a ball of positive charge with electrons dotted through it: the **plum pudding model**.
3. **Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment (1909-1911)**: Geiger and Marsden fired positively charged **alpha particles** at very thin gold foil. Most went straight through, a few were deflected, and a tiny number bounced straight back. A plum pudding could never do that. Rutherford concluded that the mass and positive charge sit in a **tiny central nucleus** and most of the atom is empty space: the **nuclear model**.
4. **Bohr** improved the nuclear model by placing electrons in **orbits (shells)** at fixed distances from the nucleus. His calculations matched experimental results.
5. Further experiments showed the positive charge of the nucleus is made of smaller particles, each with the same charge: **protons**.
6. **Chadwick (1932)** provided experimental evidence for the **neutron**, a neutral particle in the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.

The lesson here is bigger than chemistry: a scientific model is only as good as the evidence supporting it.

question.text: Put these developments of the atomic model in the order they happened, earliest first.
question.hint: The electron was found before the nucleus, and the neutron was found last of all.
question.explanation: Dalton's solid spheres came first. Thomson's discovery of the electron gave the plum pudding model. Rutherford's scattering experiment gave the nuclear model, Bohr then added fixed orbits, and Chadwick found the neutron in 1932.
order: Atoms are described as tiny solid spheres that cannot be divided
The electron is discovered and the plum pudding model is proposed
Alpha particles scattered by gold foil show that the atom has a tiny positive nucleus
Electrons are placed in orbits at fixed distances from the nucleus
Experimental evidence for the neutron is found

activities.title: Inside the atom
activities.content:
## Subatomic particles

| Particle | Relative charge | Relative mass | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Proton** | +1 | 1 | Nucleus |
| **Neutron** | 0 | 1 | Nucleus |
| **Electron** | −1 | very small (about 1/2000) | Shells around the nucleus |

An atom has **no overall charge** because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

## Size

Atoms are tiny: the radius of an atom is about **0.1 nm** (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m). The nucleus is far smaller still, less than **1/10 000** of the radius of the atom (about 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m), yet it holds almost all the mass.

## Atomic number and mass number

- **Atomic number** = number of protons. This defines the element: every atom with 6 protons is carbon.
- **Mass number** = protons + neutrons.

In the symbol ²³₁₁Na the top number (23) is the mass number and the bottom number (11) is the atomic number. So a sodium atom has 11 protons, 11 electrons and 23 − 11 = **12 neutrons**.

## Ions

When an atom **loses or gains electrons** it becomes a charged **ion**. The protons never change. Mg²⁺ still has 12 protons but only 10 electrons (12 − 2). O²⁻ has 8 protons and 10 electrons (8 + 2).

question.text: An atom of bromine is represented as ⁸¹₃₅Br. How many neutrons does this atom contain?

activities.title: Isotopes, relative atomic mass and electron shells
activities.content:
## Isotopes

**Isotopes** are atoms of the **same element** (same number of protons) with **different numbers of neutrons**, and so different mass numbers. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons, but carbon-14 has 8 neutrons instead of 6. Isotopes react in the same way because they have identical electrons; only their masses differ.

## Relative atomic mass (Ar)

Because a natural sample contains a mix of isotopes, the periodic table shows an **average mass**, weighted by how common each isotope is. Relative atomic mass is measured on a scale where an atom of carbon-12 has a mass of exactly 12.

$A_r = \frac{(\text{mass}_1 \times \text{abundance}_1) + (\text{mass}_2 \times \text{abundance}_2)}{100}$

A weighted mean always lies between the isotope masses, closer to the more abundant one.

## Electronic structure

Electrons sit in **shells** (energy levels) around the nucleus. The lowest shell fills first.

- 1st shell: up to **2** electrons
- 2nd shell: up to **8**
- 3rd shell: up to **8** (for the first 20 elements)

Write the structure as numbers separated by commas. Oxygen (8 electrons) is 2,6. Phosphorus (15) is 2,8,5. The number of occupied shells tells you the **period**, and the electrons in the outer shell tell you the **group** (for Groups 1 to 7).

activities.title: Worked example: Ar of chlorine and an electronic structure
activities.content:
**Part 1. A sample of chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. Calculate its relative atomic mass.**

1. Multiply each mass by its percentage: 35 × 75 = 2625 and 37 × 25 = 925
2. Add them: 2625 + 925 = 3550
3. Divide by 100: 3550 ÷ 100 = **35.5**

Sense check: 35.5 lies between 35 and 37, and nearer to 35 because chlorine-35 is more common. That is exactly why the periodic table gives chlorine an Ar of 35.5.

**Part 2. Write the electronic structure of calcium (atomic number 20).**

1. A neutral atom has 20 electrons.
2. Fill the shells in order: 2 in the first, 8 in the second, 8 in the third. That uses 18.
3. The remaining 2 go in the fourth shell.

Electronic structure: **2,8,8,2**. Four shells means Period 4; two outer electrons means Group 2.

question.text: Rubidium has two isotopes: rubidium-85 with an abundance of 72% and rubidium-87 with an abundance of 28%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of rubidium. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
question.hint: Multiply each mass by its percentage, add the two results, then divide by 100.

question.text:
Sulfur has several isotopes. One of them is represented as ³⁴₁₆S.

(a) What is meant by the term **isotopes**? (1 mark)

(b) Give the number of protons, electrons and neutrons in one atom of ³⁴₁₆S. (2 marks)

(c) Write the electronic structure of a sulfur atom. (1 mark)
question.hint: The bottom number gives protons (and electrons in a neutral atom). Subtract it from the top number for neutrons. Then fill shells 2, 8, then the rest.
question.explanation: (a) Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. (b) Atomic number 16 so 16 protons and 16 electrons; neutrons = 34 − 16 = 18. (c) 16 electrons: 2,8,6.

markScheme.criterion: (a) Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Elements** contain one type of atom; **compounds** contain elements chemically bonded; **mixtures** are not bonded and can be separated physically (filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation, chromatography).
- Symbol equations must **balance**: change the big numbers, never the subscripts.
- The atomic model went: solid spheres → plum pudding → nuclear model (alpha scattering) → Bohr orbits → protons → neutron (Chadwick).
- Proton +1 (mass 1), neutron 0 (mass 1), electron −1 (tiny mass). Atom radius ≈ 0.1 nm; nucleus < 1/10 000 of that.
- **Atomic number** = protons; **mass number** = protons + neutrons; neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
- **Isotopes**: same protons, different neutrons. Ar = Σ(mass × abundance) ÷ 100.
- Electron shells fill 2, 8, 8 for the first 20 elements.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a compound can be separated into its elements by filtration.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about whether the elements in a compound are chemically bonded.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. In a compound the elements are chemically bonded, so a chemical reaction is needed to separate them. Filtration is a physical process that only separates mixtures.

options.feedback: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid in a mixture, not bonded elements.

practiceQuestions.text: Which is the correct chemical symbol for sodium?
practiceQuestions.hint: The symbol comes from the Latin name natrium.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sodium is Na. S is sulfur, N is nitrogen, and So is not a symbol for any element. Only the first letter of a symbol is a capital.

metadata.blanksText: The ___ number of an atom is the number of protons it contains, while the ___ number is the total number of protons and neutrons.

practiceQuestions.hint: One of these words is also the name of a very small particle; the other describes how heavy something is.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The atomic number is the number of protons. The mass number is protons plus neutrons.

practiceQuestions.text: Iron has atomic number 26. How many neutrons are in an atom of iron-56?
practiceQuestions.hint: The 56 in iron-56 is the mass number.

practiceQuestions.text: A sample of copper contains 69% copper-63 and 31% copper-65. Calculate the relative atomic mass of copper. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
Match each term to its correct description.
practiceQuestions.hint: Two of the descriptions are about bonding; two are about the particles inside atoms.
practiceQuestions.explanation: An element has one type of atom. A compound has two or more elements bonded together. A mixture is not chemically joined. Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons.

pairs.right: A substance made of only one type of atom
Two or more elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions
Two or more substances that are not chemically joined
Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these conclusions came from the alpha particle scattering experiment? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what happened to most alpha particles and what happened to a very few.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space. A few were deflected or bounced back, which showed a concentrated positive charge and most of the mass in a tiny nucleus. The plum pudding idea was rejected, and electrons are not in the nucleus.

options.text: The atom is mostly empty space
The positive charge is concentrated in a tiny central nucleus
Most of the mass of the atom is in the nucleus
The atom is a ball of positive charge with electrons spread through it
options.feedback: That is the plum pudding model, which this experiment disproved.

options.text: Electrons are found inside the nucleus

practiceQuestions.text: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes. Explain why they have identical chemical reactions but different masses.
practiceQuestions.hint: Chemical reactions depend on electrons; mass depends on what is in the nucleus.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Both isotopes have 17 protons and therefore 17 electrons in the same arrangement (2,8,7), so they react identically. Chlorine-37 has two more neutrons than chlorine-35, so its atoms have a greater mass.

markScheme.criterion: Same number of electrons / same electronic structure, so same chemical properties
Different numbers of neutrons, so different mass

practiceQuestions.text:
Gallium (atomic number 31) has two naturally occurring isotopes: gallium-69 with an abundance of 60% and gallium-71 with an abundance of 40%.

(a) Calculate the relative atomic mass of gallium. Show your working and give your answer to 1 decimal place. (2 marks)

(b) State the number of protons and the number of electrons in a Ga³⁺ ion. (1 mark)

(c) Explain why atoms of gallium-69 and gallium-71 react in the same way. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a) multiply each mass by its percentage and divide the total by 100. For (b) a 3+ ion has lost three electrons.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) 69 × 60 = 4140 and 71 × 40 = 2840. Total 6980 ÷ 100 = 69.8. (b) 31 protons; 31 − 3 = 28 electrons. (c) Both isotopes have the same number of electrons (same electronic structure), and chemical reactions only involve electrons.

markScheme.criterion: (c) Same number of electrons / same electronic structure

practiceQuestions.text: A student wants to obtain dry copper sulfate crystals from copper sulfate solution. Put the steps in the correct order.
practiceQuestions.hint: You need to remove some water before crystals can form, and crystals grow as the solution cools.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pour the solution into an evaporating basin, heat gently to drive off some water until crystals begin to appear, leave to cool so the crystals grow, then filter and dry them.
order: Pour the solution into an evaporating basin
Heat gently until crystals start to form at the edge of the basin
Leave the solution to cool so that crystals grow
Filter off the crystals and pat them dry with filter paper

practiceQuestions.text: Which pair of particles are isotopes of the same element?
practiceQuestions.hint: Isotopes must have the same bottom number (atomic number) but a different top number (mass number).
practiceQuestions.explanation: ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl both have 17 protons but 18 and 20 neutrons respectively, so they are isotopes. ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca have the same mass number but are different elements. ²³₁₁Na and ²³₁₁Na⁺ are the same atom, one of which has lost an electron. ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₇N are different elements.

options.feedback: Same mass number, but different atomic numbers means different elements.
These have the same numbers of protons and neutrons; the ion has simply lost an electron.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the electronic structure of aluminium (atomic number 13).

metadata.blanksText: Aluminium has 13 electrons, so its electronic structure is 2, ___, ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Fill the second shell completely before starting the third.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 13 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, leaving 3 for the third. Electronic structure 2,8,3.
